title: The Englund Gambit
description: The famous, fun gambit against White's 1.d4 which can get you a checkmate in 8 moves. Obviously a bit more dubious as you rise up the rating ladder, but for beginners: epic!

N1bk1bnr/p2p1ppp/8/1p2q3/8/2P5/PP2PPPP/R.text: We're winning the knight and we'll end up with a material advantage.

N1bk1bnr/pp1p1ppp/2n5/4P3/4q3/5N2/PPP1PP.text:
White takes the rook.

Let's regain the pawn on e5.

N1bk1bnr/pp1p1ppp/8/4N3/4q3/8/PPP1PPPP/R.text:
White trades.

We capture on e5. We are now threatening a nasty tactic with Bb4+ 11.c3 Bxc3+! and White loses lots of material.

r1b1k1nr/2p2ppp/p1p2b2/3p3Q/8/4P3/P1PN1P.text:
White castles.

Let's get the last piece out into the game, with a sneaky idea in mind.

r1b1k1nr/2p2ppp/p1p5/3pb2Q/8/4P3/P1PN1PP.text:
Developing the queen and attacking our bishop.

Our bishop drops back into safety on f6.

r1b1k1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B1pb3/8/4P3/P1PN1P.text:
Pinning the knight.

We'll challenge the bishop.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/1B6/5N2/PqP1PP.text: Choosing to exchange pieces to get rid of the pressure.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/1b6/2B2N2/P1P1.text:
White will get our queen and is definitely better, but on the other hand, Black has some counterplay and piece coordination.

Definitely worth a try if you are intent on seriously surprising your opponent in a blitz game!

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/1b6/2B2N2/PqPQ.text:
White defends c3. But this falls into the most famous Englund Gambit trap.

We'll take on c3.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/1b6/2N2N2/PqPB.text:
White attacks our queen.

We are going to sacrifice our queen on c3!

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/8/2b5/P1PNPPPP.text: Either way, you'll be able to get the central pawn back, which is nice.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4b3/8/4P3/P1PN1PPP.text:
White gets ready to develop the light-squared bishop.

We'll get ready to develop further.

Let's examine a possible continuation.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/1n6/5N2/PqP1PPPP.text: But we're simply crashing through on c2.

r1b1k2r/2p2ppp/p1p2b1n/3p3Q/4P3/8/P1PN1P.text:
e4 fails to do anything about our idea.

And out comes our bishop. The queen is trapped!

r1b1kbnr/pp1pqppp/2p5/4n3/4P3/2N2N2/PPP1.text:
The bishop is developed.

We'll make room for the c8-bishop to get into the game.

r1b1kbnr/pp2qp1p/2pp2p1/4n3/4P3/2N2N2/PP.text: And we're continuing with standard development, soon castling short.

r1b1kbnr/ppNp1ppp/2n5/4P3/4q3/5N2/PPP1PP.text:
Check!

We move to d8, with the point that the knight can't get out after it takes the rook.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/3NP3/5q2/5N2/PPP1P.text:
Our queen and c7 pawn are forked.

We'll get the queen out of danger.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/1q3B2/2N2N2/PP.text:
White blocks the check and thinks they're setting a trap. 

This move is played 14% of the time.

We are not afraid, and we capture the bishop.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/1q6/5N2/PPPBPP.text:
White blocks and attacks our queen 60% of the time.

We capture on b2.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/8/2B2N2/PqP1PP.text:
This move attacks our queen and defends the rook, and it's played 24% of the time

It seems attractive to attack the queen in the corner, but this gives us a winning advantage.

We bring our bishop into the game, with a decisive pin!

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/8/2N2N2/PqPBPP.text:
White simply develops and argues we have lost too much time. 

This move is by far the most common, played 76% of the time.

Black now adds pressure to the knight.

r1b1kbnr/ppppqppp/2n5/4P3/5B2/5N2/PPP1PP.text:
White adds another defender. But that was sort of the plan! Because we do have a plan. 

In any case, they'll defend the pawn like this 34% of the time, which is more than 3.2 million games.

We give check with the queen, also hitting the f4-bishop and the b2-pawn.

r1b1kbnr/ppppqppp/2n5/4P3/8/2N2N2/PPP1PP.text:
White just develops a piece 21% of the time.

This allows us to take on e5.

r1b1kbnr/ppppqppp/8/4n3/4P3/2N2N2/PPP2PP.text:
White places a pawn in the center.

We'll take measures to prevent the potentially irritating Nd5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/8/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
White tries to hold onto the pawn on e5. 

In the beginning, our play revolves around trying to grab it back.

r3k2r/2p2ppp/p1p2b2/3p4/4P1n1/8/P1PN1PPP.text:
But we can recapture, and this is one of those odd times in which you could win after White plays the first moves well. 

White might try to push you around with h3, f4 and e5. 

But don't be scared! You're up a piece and winning easily.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/8/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
White accepts it, obviously.

We proceed with rapid development.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the Englund Gambit! 

Now, against 1. d4, you've got a surprise weapon with the Englund! 

Not particularly sound, and even with a variation where you trade a queen for not quite enough material, this opening can get tricky in shorter time controls and against opponents who aren't well-prepared.
